posts.title: Building your first dashboard from scratch
posts.excerpt: What to model, what to leave out, and how to keep the dashboard from rotting after launch.
posts.author: Stoic Finch
posts.content:
# Building your first dashboard from scratch

The first dashboard a company ships is almost always wrong. Not because the team is bad — because the team hasn't yet learned what _their_ dashboard needs to be.

Here's the playbook we use when a client asks us to build their first dashboard.

## Start with the meeting it replaces

Dashboards don't live in a vacuum. They replace something — a spreadsheet, a slide, a recurring meeting. Find that thing first. The new dashboard inherits its audience, its cadence, and most of its definitions.

If nothing's being replaced, ask harder. Net-new dashboards almost never get adopted.

## Model before you draw

The biggest single lever on dashboard quality is the data model behind it. Not the visualization. Not the BI tool. The model.

For a first dashboard we keep the model conservative:

- **One fact table** — the events you actually want to count.
- **Three to five conformed dimensions** — the slicers leadership cares about (date, segment, product, region, owner).
- **Three to five metrics** — defined in code (dbt model, semantic layer), not in the BI tool.

Define the metrics _once_, in code, with comments. If 'revenue' has three definitions in the dashboard, you've already lost.

## Leave things out

A dashboard with 18 charts has zero charts. The eye doesn't know where to land. The reviewer asks, 'what am I looking at?'

Most first dashboards we ship have **four to six visualizations**. One headline KPI. Two or three trend charts. One or two breakdowns. That's it. Everything else lives in linked drill-through pages.

## Keep it from rotting

Dashboards rot. Pipelines fail silently. Definitions drift. The Monday-morning user notices that 'something's off' and the trust evaporates.

Before launch, every dashboard we ship has:

1. **Freshness checks** — automated assertions that the source data updated within SLA.
2. **Volume checks** — assertions that row counts are within the expected band.
3. **Definition tests** — at least one regression test per metric, in dbt.
4. **An owner** — a named person whose job description includes 'this dashboard works'.

No owner, no dashboard. We've stopped shipping things to clients who don't have one.

## Ship in three weeks

A first dashboard, done right, is a three-week engagement:

- Week 1 — interview the audience, define the model and metrics.
- Week 2 — build the model, write the tests, build the dashboard.
- Week 3 — review with stakeholders, iterate, hand over.

More than three weeks and you're probably building the wrong thing. Less than three and you skipped one of the steps that prevents the rot.

---

posts.title: When to hire a data team vs. embed one
posts.excerpt: A decision framework for mid-market companies trying to figure out whether to build or borrow.
posts.author: Stoic Finch
posts.content:
# When to hire a data team vs. embed one

Mid-market companies (50-500 people) hit the same fork every couple of years: do we hire a data team, or do we bring in outside specialists?

There isn't one right answer. There are signals.

## Hire when…

- Your data work is **continuous and well-understood** — daily reports, monthly close, recurring analyses you already know how to do.
- You have **someone senior internal to manage them** — junior analysts without a senior data lead are an expensive way to ship spreadsheets.
- The work is **proprietary** — domain knowledge is the constraint, not technical skill.
- You can **fund the role for 18+ months** — hiring data people, training them, and losing them in 9 months is the worst outcome.

## Embed when…

- You need **specific expertise for a specific phase** — set up a warehouse, build the first dashboards, deploy the first model.
- You don't yet know **what you're hiring for** — the right answer to 'we need a data person' is sometimes 'we need an engineer', sometimes 'an analyst', sometimes 'a PM'. Embedding helps you find out.
- The work is **bursty** — three months heavy, then quiet for six.
- You want **hire-able patterns** — a good consulting engagement leaves you with code, documentation, and a job description for the right next hire.

## The hybrid that works

Most successful mid-market data functions are a permanent senior data lead + an external boutique on retainer for specific phases. The lead owns continuity and relationships. The boutique brings horsepower and specific expertise when the moment calls for it.

The pattern that doesn't work: senior data lead, no team, no budget for outside help. They burn out in 14 months.

## A simple test

Before you commit either way, write down:

1. The next three things you want a data team to do.
2. Whether each is **continuous** or **one-time**.
3. Whether each requires **deep domain knowledge** or **technical depth**.

If the list is mostly continuous + domain — hire. If it's mostly one-time + technical — embed. If it's mixed (most are) — do both.

---

posts.title: Five signs your reporting is costing you a half-FTE
posts.excerpt: If you can check off three of these, you're losing 20+ hours a week to reporting overhead.
posts.author: Stoic Finch
posts.content:
# Five signs your reporting is costing you a half-FTE

Reporting overhead is sneaky. It hides in calendars, in 'just one quick spreadsheet', in the analyst who 'doesn't mind' staying late on Monday.

Here are the five signs we look for. Three or more and you're losing a half-FTE — minimum.

## 1. Someone exports a CSV every week

If any human action is required between 'data exists' and 'leadership sees it', that human is your reporting bottleneck. Worse: every export is a chance to make a mistake.

The fix is rarely 'a better export' — it's 'no export'. Pipe the source into a warehouse and let the BI tool refresh on a schedule.

## 2. Numbers don't match across decks

Finance has revenue at 4.2M. Sales has it at 4.5M. Ops has it at 4.18M. They're all 'right' — just defined differently.

This is a metric-definition problem, not a Power BI problem. Every metric needs to live in code (dbt or a semantic layer) with one definition. The deck reads from there. Not the other way around.

## 3. The Monday meeting starts with 'let me refresh'

If the dashboard isn't ready when the meeting starts, the dashboard isn't really shipping. People are doing reporting in real-time, manually, in front of an audience.

Fix: scheduled refresh, ideally 30 minutes before any recurring meeting that uses the data.

## 4. Adding one chart takes a week

A mature reporting setup adds a new chart in an afternoon. If yours takes a week, the model is the bottleneck — usually because it doesn't exist and the analyst is rebuilding logic from scratch each time.

Fix: a modelled warehouse with reusable marts. dbt is the standard for this.

## 5. The analyst can't take vacation

The acid test. If your reporting depends on one person being at their keyboard, you don't have a reporting function — you have a brittle hostage situation.

Fix: documentation, automation, and a deliberate runbook. If the analyst is sick, leadership should still get their Monday email.

## What it costs

A conservative half-FTE at a mid-market analyst rate is about CAD 50,000 / year of pure reporting overhead. Not analysis. Not insight. Overhead.

Most of it can be eliminated in a 4-6 week engagement.

---
